.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 128 PM EST Monday...

1. Warm temperatures continue through Wednesday with potential

2. Light rain showers are possible on Tuesday afternoon and 
evening, then widespread rain is expected Thursday into Friday 
morning.

3. Precip lingers for several days behind the cold front

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 128 PM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure 1034 mb centered over the mid Atlantic 
coast this afternoon will continue to drift slowly eastward into the 
Atlantic Ocean this week, turning flow over northern New York and 
Vermont more southerly. This will result in a warming trend today 
through Wednesday, although some shower chances towards the Canadian 
border Tuesday afternoon may stunt warmth locally, particularly 
along the international border. Highs on Tuesday will be widespread 
60s with overnight lows in the mid 40s to lower 50s. The warmest day 
of the week will be Wednesday with deep layer winds advecting warm 
air out of the south/southeasterly directions under mostly clear to 
partly cloudy skies. Low and mid 70s are anticipated for Wednesday 
afternoon, with lows that night as warm as the 40s to mid 50s. A few 
spots could exceed their daily records, particularly in the St. 
Lawrence Valley of New York. Warmth recedes slightly on Thursday, 
but conditions remain warm with widespread highs in the 60s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A weak wave will be moving along a ridge's northern 
periphery Tuesday and Tuesday night, bringing rain shower chances 
mainly to northern New York and the northern half of Vermont. 
Amounts will be light given that it will be moving into a ridge, 
with projected rainfall up to 0.15 inches at most, highest along the 
international border. Breezy southerly winds are also likely in 
north south oriented valleys Tuesday night after the showers pass 
through. Then on Thursday, rain will spread eastward through our 
region, driven by a frontal boundary attached to an elongated low 
pressure stretched from the Great Lakes to Quebec, Canada. Winds 
will be breezy out of the south with gusts up to 20-25 mph, 
particularly Thursday morning ahead of steady precipitation. Most 
likely period for rainfall is Thursday for northern New York, then 
Thursday night for Vermont. Some upslope flow could mean highest 
precipitation amounts on western slopes of the Adirondacks and 
Greens. Precipitation amounts in 24 hours reaching a half inch or 
more look fairly unlikely, with perhaps the best chance of these 
higher amounts in the Adirondacks and southern half of Vermont, 
closest to the stream of moisture coming off the Gulf. All 
precipitation should be rain with this system, and we're not 
expecting a dramatic cooldown until at least this weekend. More on 
the extended forecast below.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Following Friday's frontal passage, we'll have several 
days of active weather. A secondary low pressure forms downstream of 
the front. This secondary low will meander eastward with precip 
rotating around the center of the low. At this point, we can't nail 
down the timing but expect chance to likely rain from Friday evening 
through Sunday. One of the questions we will need to answer is how 
quickly that secondary low moves. If it moves quickly, Friday and 
Saturday will be largely wet while Sunday will be drier. If the 
system is more cutoff and slower moving, Sunday will trend wetter. 
Either way, we should see multiple inches of rain over the period 
which will help mitigate the expanding drought we've been seeing.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Through 18Z Tuesday...VFR will continue with moderate southwest winds
through the daylight hours. Surface winds will decrease 
overnight, but winds aloft will prevent any fog formation. 
Clouds will move in from the northwest tomorrow morning, with 
MVFR ceilings possible by 15z at SLK. Light rain will start at 
MSS by 16z.
